articles.title: L.A.'s next mayor faces high expectations, little room for error
articles.summary: Whoever becomes the next mayor of L.A., she will face a slew of challenges: homelessness, affordable housing, potholes, streetlights, the Olympics, unstable...
articles.body:
Homeless encampments line the streets. Buying a home — or even finding an affordable place to rent — is increasingly out of reach. Roads are riddled with potholes, tens of thousands of streetlights are out , and water and power bills are surging .

For many Angelenos, morale is poor and quality of life in the city is slipping.

This is the challenge for whomever becomes Los Angeles mayor — and it is one that has left some longtime political experts wondering how much one person can control in this vast city of 3.8 million.

"The expectations, given the powers that the mayor actually has, are probably too high," said Tom Hogen-Esch, a professor of political science at Cal State Northridge. "You have all of these wicked problems that are difficult to solve in a perfect scenario, and [even more] in a governmental system as tangled and confused as L.A."

The next mayor will have to deal with enduring problems of deteriorating infrastructure , police reform and budget woes. But there is also the unprecedented task of rebuilding Pacific Palisades after catastrophic firestorms and trying to help the city's ailing film industry — all while preparing the city for the global spotlight of hosting the 2028 Olympics.

A recent UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll of likely L.A. voters, co-sponsored by The Times, found that the top priority for the next mayor to address was reducing the number of homeless encampments, followed by ensuring public safety and building more affordable housing. Protecting immigrant communities was the next most cited concern, followed by balancing the city budget.

After studying L.A. politics for more than three decades, Hogen-Esch said the city feels stuck.

"We're talking about the same issues over and over and over ... and a general underlying frustration with city government," he said. "It's almost like you could wake up 30 years later in a Rip Van Winkle dream and you're in the same spot."

When Karen Bass launched her 2021 mayoral campaign, she proclaimed homelessness was her "overwhelming top priority."

After nearly four years of her leadership, she has failed to make a serious dent on homelessness. This year, the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority announced that more than 45,194 people in the city were homeless — not significantly different from 46,260 homeless people in January 2023.

After spending more than $391 million on Inside Safe , Bass' flagship program to clean up homeless encampments and house homeless people, the city moved about 6,500 people into interim housing. But about 42% of the program's participants have returned to homelessness.

Bass insists Inside Safe has made progress, clearing 140 encampments across the city. But the difference is not visible to many residents as more encampments continue to block city sidewalks.

Over the last four years, L.A. budgeted about $4 billion to address the homeless crisis — about $100,000 for every homeless person in the city, according to Lee Ohanian, a professor of economics at UCLA.

But the city has not spent all that money. L.A. underspent its homelessness budget by at least $473 million in the 2025-26 fiscal year, L.A. City Controller Kenneth Mejia said , because of its decentralized approach to homelessness, budget structure, staffing shortages and long approval delays for affordable housing.

Part of the challenge in addressing homelessness is that L.A. adopts a fragmented approach, sharing responsibility with the county and spreading programs among different nonprofits, said Fernando Guerra, founding director of the Center for the Study of Los Angeles at Loyola Marymount University. Unlike in New York, the L.A. mayor does not oversee the health department, mental health and drug recovery programs, and jails.

"The challenge for the mayor has always been that she or he is only given basically half of the arsenal to fight homelessness," Guerra said.

Poor oversight is also a problem. Federal prosecutors have charged multiple nonprofit leaders with defrauding taxpayer funds meant to support the homeless. Last month, a nonprofit chief executive pleaded guilty to wire fraud and embezzling $23 million in homeless funds to pay for a $7-million Westwood home and vacation property in Greece.

But perhaps the biggest challenge is the staggering cost of building housing for homeless people in L.A.. Because of complex government financing, prevailing wage requirements, environmental rules, and the integration of medical and social services, a single unit in L.A. can cost as much as $600,000.

Nearly 6 out of 10 renters in L.A. are cost-burdened , and polls show a majority of L.A. voters have considered leaving the city because housing is so expensive.

Bass has taken steps to accelerate the building of affordable housing. Her signature program, Executive Directive One , succeeded in cutting the time it takes to review 100% affordable projects and led to a flurry of development proposals. But after tenant advocates warned that rent-controlled apartments would be demolished and homeowners complained that density threatened historic neighborhoods, Bass restricted the locations eligible for the program .

Nearly four years after Bass took office, developers are not exactly seeing a building boom . Last month, the mayor's office said more than 47,000 units of affordable housing are in the pipeline, but only 7,728 are under construction.

As with homelessness, the mayor has limited power to improve affordability.

A big test for the new mayor will be the state's push to pass laws that spur more housing, such as state Senate Bill 79, designed to accelerate development around transportation hubs. With new buildings likely to face opposition in many parts of the city, Bass has opposed SB 79, arguing that it will erode local control.

Whoever the next mayor is, they will have to balance the need to build significantly more housing with homeowner opposition to new development, said Christian Grose, a professor of political science and public policy at USC.

"Voters probably are somewhere in the middle," Grose said, "and there doesn't seem to be a policy agenda that reaches those voters."

When Chief Deputy City Controller Rick Cole retired from City Hall last year, he complained that "mind-numbing bureaucracy" had made the city ungovernable. Los Angeles was paying for city leaders' decision long ago to organize the city to disperse authority, he said, citing deteriorating city infrastructure as a key example.

"Beneath the broken sidewalks," Cole said, "is a broken system."

More than 5,000 requests for sidewalk repairs are pending. Tens of thousands of streetlights are out . Last year, the city stopped repaving streets for eight months as officials struggled with staffing shortages to meet federal requirements to construct curb ramps for wheelchairs and new city rules that mandate bike, bus and pedestrian enhancements.

"The city can't seem to manage the basics," Bass' challenger, City Councilwoman Nithya Raman, said when she announced her campaign in February.

Guerra said it was astounding that such a large city government — with a $14.8-billion budget and more than 5,500 public works employees — was so behind on fixing streetlights and resurfacing roads.

"How could that be?" Guerra said. "You cannot tell us that you need more people and more money to do this. What is happening?"

To speed up infrastructure repairs, some public officials are urging voters to pass Measure LA , which would require the city to develop a long-term capital infrastructure plan and distribute more power to the director of public works. Supporters say the measure would cut systemic bureaucracy and fragmentation. Critics, however, say it would lead to one person holding too much authority.

Last year, the City Council and mayor declared a fiscal state of emergency as they faced a $1-billion deficit due to revenue shortfalls as well as increased liabilities from the Palisades fire. Rating agencies, including S&P and Kroll, downgraded the city to a " negative" outlook.

Mejia cited ongoing revenue shortfalls, liability payouts and departmental overspending as the key reasons for the ballooning budget, which has grown by about 25% over the last four years.

The Bass administration has increased pay and benefits to thousands of city employees and police officers . It has also had to hand out record liability settlement payments due to LAPD excessive force claims and dangerous street and transport conditions.

Raman, a democratic socialist, has frequently voted against high city spending, opposing pay raises negotiated by Bass for Los Angeles Police Department officers and the $2.6-billion expansion of the Los Angeles Convention Center .

"She's the one that says, 'We cannot afford that. How are you going to pay for that?' " Guerra said of Raman. "It's very, very strange that the socialist is the fiscal hawk."

Violent crime in L.A. has plummeted. Last month, Bass announced a 47% drop in homicides since she took office, and she has also touted a decline in property crime such as burglaries .

But police reform and police pay remain issues. While Raman has reversed her past stance on defunding the police, she has stated she would replace LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell, who she says has " lost the confidence " of Angelenos on the issue of immigration. The city, she says, needs a police chief who ensures officers do not cooperate with federal immigration officers. She has vowed to conduct an audit of the department to determine whether there are gaps between Los Angeles' "sanctuary city" policies and police practices.

Bass has publicly backed McDonnell, supporting his efforts to stem officer attrition and rebuild the department's ranks. The department would be significantly disrupted, she has argued, if the chief were removed before the 2028 Olympic Games.

The new mayor will also face a challenge that is harder to qualify: making residents believe City Hall can fix Los Angeles' many problems.

"I think we're beyond pessimism in some places," Hogen-Esch said, noting that for the first time in a quarter of a century he has spotted no mayoral campaign signs in his El Sereno neighborhood.

When it comes to homelessness, Angelenos would be happy to spend money if it actually solved the problem, said Jim Newton, a veteran journalist and editor of UCLA Blueprint magazine. Most want encampments gone for good, and not by locking people up or punishing them for being poor, but by genuinely helping them to be better.

"Is that possible?" he said. "I don't know."

Others say it will take new ideas and big swings that can be challenging in a city where the mayor has only limited powers.

"When they first took power, they were incredibly innovative and incredibly creative," Guerra said. "Now they not only lack creativity and innovation in Los Angeles, but compared to other city governments, they're laggard in implementing new ideas."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: German police union defends blaming migrants groups for Gen Z riots
articles.summary: Germany's police union (GdP) pushed back on Tuesday after facing criticism for attributing violent rioting at the weekend to young men with migrant backgroun...
articles.body:
Germany's police union (GdP) pushed back on Tuesday after facing criticism for attributing violent rioting at the weekend to young men with migrant backgrounds.

Amid nationwide Gen Z protests on Saturday, rioting broke out in some cities, including incidents of violence and looting.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt pinned the blame for the unrest on "violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities," in comments echoed by other conservative politicians that triggered a political backlash.

But Andreas Rosskopf, chairman of the GdP's federal police division, defended the assertions.

"Our colleagues, who put their heads on the line for the rule of law and have done so absolutely professionally, confirm exactly these groups of perpetrators in their reports," Rosskopf told the mass-circulation Bild newspaper. He said it was incomprehensible that "attempts are being made in some political circles to gloss over this."

The late-night rioting and looting centred on the banking hub of Frankfurt. It came after thousands of young people had demonstrated peacefully for issues such as education and social policy.

Clashes with police also occurred in cities including Cologne, Hamburg and Berlin. The GdP called for swift verdicts for the offenders.

Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the Social Democrats was among those to criticize blanket accusations.

"What are migrant groups? Are they people who have lived in Germany for three generations and are German citizens? Where do we stop differentiating?" he asked on the ZDF public broadcaster.

articles.title: An unusual US housing project matches people leaving prison with homeowners willing to rent them spare rooms; it has helped more than 180 people find stable housing
articles.summary: Housing for people leaving prison is the aim of the Homecoming Project, a California scheme that matches formerly incarcerated people with homeowners
articles.body: Housing for people leaving prison is the aim of the Homecoming Project, a California scheme that matches formerly incarcerated people with homeowners willing to rent out a spare room. The model borrows from the sharing economy: hosts receive a monthly stipend, which puts extra income into communities that need it, while returnees gain a safe, welcoming place to begin rebuilding their lives. More than 180 people have secured stable housing through the scheme. Many hosts and participants have formed lasting friendships that continue long after the arrangement ends, and the project aims to change how communities welcome people back home.Why finding a safe place to live is the hardest first step for people leaving prisonImpact Justice, the organisation behind the project, argues that people leaving prison need somewhere safe and stable to live before they can look for work, tackle health problems or learn new skills. Many have no home to return to. They also face a housing market where affordable places are scarce and may be closed to anyone with a criminal record. The organisation says this sets returning citizens up to fail at the very moment they need a warm welcome.How careful screening, matching and clear agreements pair each returnee with the right hostApplicants go through a screening and matching process designed to place each participant with an eligible host. The team also helps both sides agree on clear terms from the start, so that living together stays comfortable and rewarding for everyone involved.Participants receive ongoing support, including case management and training in effective communication, problem-solving and decision-making. They also get a monthly gift card for necessities. Hosts are supported too, with vetted housemates, training opportunities and regular coaching.Where the Homecoming Project now operates across California and how homeowners can open their doorsImpact Justice says participants live in Alameda, Contra Costa and Los Angeles counties, and the project has recently expanded to San Francisco. Homeowners in any of those four counties who have a room to rent can apply to become hosts. People who know a suitable host can refer them through the referral bonus programme, and anyone who knows someone returning from prison and in need of housing can tell them about the project.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1984, a Texas school district received 640 acres of farmland; decades later, volunteer farmers are using its harvests to raise about $400,000 a year for college scholarships, helping around 300 students
articles.summary: A piece of farmland donated to a small Texas school district more than four decades ago is now helping hundreds of students pay for higher education.
articles.body: A piece of farmland donated to a small Texas school district more than four decades ago is now helping hundreds of students pay for higher education. In Gruver, a town in the Texas Panhandle, local farmers volunteer their time, machinery and farming skills to grow crops on 640 acres of donated land. The harvests generate approximately $400,000 annually for scholarships. Since the programme began awarding money in 2016, nearly $3 million has reportedly reached around 300 students.According to Texas Today, the initiative began with a decision made by Karl Nielsen, a Danish immigrant who settled in Gruver in 1901. Nielsen never married and spent much of his life living with his sister. He remained in the town until his death in 1984, at the age of 105. Before his death, he decided to leave 640 acres, equivalent to one square mile, to the Gruver Independent School District.For several years, the school district earned about $25,000 annually by leasing the property. The money helped purchase educational supplies, including books and science equipment. However, the land's potential to support students remained largely unused until two local residents discussed a different approach.Around 2012, then-school superintendent David Teal and farmer Chad Logsdon discussed the property while sitting in a pickup truck at a football game. Teal believed the district could earn considerably more by farming the land instead of leasing it. He proposed using the income to help local students attend college or trade school. Logsdon supported the idea, and the Gruver Farm Scholarship Foundation was established that year.Local farmers turn land into scholarship fundThe foundation developed a system in which farmers could contribute their agricultural skills without receiving payment for their work. Each year, a lead farmer would coordinate volunteers responsible for planting, harvesting and transporting crops to market.Farmers offered their tractors, equipment, diesel and labour. Agricultural companies contributed seeds and fertilisers, while residents and local businesses provided additional financial support. Banks, insurance companies and feedlots also became involved.The arrangement meant that the foundation could use resources already available within the community rather than paying for every stage of agricultural production.The volunteers grow corn and wheat on the property. According to Texas Today, the farming operation now generates approximately $400,000 annually for scholarships.However, the foundation did not begin distributing money immediately. It spent four years building its funds, accumulating nearly $1 million before the first scholarships were awarded.First students received scholarships in 2016The first beneficiaries were students graduating from Gruver in 2016. That year, the foundation distributed $350,000 towards college and trade school tuition.Recipients enrolled at different institutions, including West Texas A&M University and Texas Tech University. Others pursued technical education, including diesel mechanics training at WyoTech in Laramie, Wyoming.Students qualify through a points-based system that considers more than academic performance. Their grades, extracurricular activities and community participation all contribute towards eligibility.Participation in sports, cheerleading and school bands can earn points. Students can also receive credit for activities such as theatre and debate. Community service is another consideration, with students earning points for completing 25 hours annually. Such work can include mowing lawns for elderly residents or helping arrange tables for a church picnic.Explaining the programme's wider purpose, Gruver ISD superintendent Wade Callaway told Texas Standard, “we are growing graduates and we are growing good neighbors.”The foundation also supports further education beyond an undergraduate degree. Students who complete college within four years may qualify for assistance towards a Master's degree. Teachers working in the district can also receive support for postgraduate studies.Nearly $3 million awarded to around 300 studentsThe programme has continued to expand since its first scholarships were awarded. Texas Standard reported in November 2024 that the foundation had distributed $2.5 million to 277 students. Its report also found that 59 scholarship recipients graduated from college between 2016 and 2020, including 23 first-generation college students.More recent figures published by Texas Today in November this year put the total at nearly $3 million distributed to approximately 300 students. Individual scholarship awards can reach about $40,000.The newer report also stated that approximately 48 recipients had become first-generation college graduates. Some beneficiaries have subsequently returned to the Texas Panhandle to work in agriculture, education and healthcare, including as farmers, teachers and nurses.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Georgia company paid $220,000 at a tax auction for an Atlanta parcel it says does not exist; after demanding its money back, it lost an October 30 appeal because the county was protected by sovereign immunity
articles.summary: Paying hundreds of thousands of dollars for a property that a buyer later claims does not physically exist can turn a tax auction into a costly legal
articles.body: Paying hundreds of thousands of dollars for a property that a buyer later claims does not physically exist can turn a tax auction into a costly legal dispute. A Georgia company that spent $220,000 to purchase an Atlanta parcel through a county tax sale found itself fighting to recover the money after questioning whether the land listed in the auction records was real. However, its attempt to obtain a refund from Fulton County has faced a major legal obstacle.In its October 30, 2026, decision in Talon Assets, LLC v. Fulton County, available on Justia, the Georgia Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal of the company's lawsuit, ruling that sovereign immunity protected the county from the relief Talon had requested. The court found that the company's declaratory judgment petition did not qualify for the limited constitutional waiver of sovereign immunity because it sought repayment of the $220,000 and cancellation of the tax deed rather than permissible declaratory and injunctive relief. However, the judges directed the lower court to dismiss the case without prejudice rather than with prejudice.How the $220,000 tax auction purchase happenedThe dispute began with a tax sale conducted by the Fulton County Sheriff on June 6, 2023. The auction involved a parcel on Sims Street in Atlanta, identified by parcel number 14-0087-0008-025-6. The property was owned by Marathon Holdings, LLC, which was the defendant in the tax execution proceedings. Talon Assets emerged as the highest bidder at the auction and paid $220,000 to the Fulton County Sheriff in exchange for a tax deed. However, Talon later questioned whether the property described in the auction records actually existed.According to the company's allegations, the Fulton County Board of Assessors had mistakenly created the parcel in its mapping systems even though there was no corresponding physical property. Talon claimed that this mapping error led the Fulton County Tax Commissioner's Office to issue tax liens against the parcel and ultimately resulted in the sheriff conducting a tax sale over unpaid taxes. The company argued that the tax deed was therefore invalid because it related to a parcel that did not physically exist.Company demands its money backOn September 15, 2023, Talon sent an email to Eugene Smith, an attorney representing the Fulton County Sheriff, demanding the return of the $220,000 and cancellation of the tax deed. The company also made a money rule demand under Georgia law to the sheriff and the Fulton County Board of Commissioners. However, it did not receive reimbursement. Talon subsequently filed a petition for declaratory judgment in Fulton County Superior Court. It asked the court to declare the tax deed void from the beginning and direct the county to return the money paid at the auction.Fulton County opposed the lawsuit and sought its dismissal. The county disputed the company's assertion that the parcel did not exist, maintaining that the property was real and that the tax deed described it sufficiently. The county also argued that the lawsuit was barred by sovereign immunity, a legal protection that generally prevents government entities from being sued without their consent. The trial court agreed with the county and dismissed Talon's petition. The company then appealed the decision, arguing that its request for declaratory relief was covered by a constitutional exception to sovereign immunity.Why sovereign immunity became the central issueThe Georgia Constitution provides a limited waiver of sovereign immunity for certain lawsuits seeking declaratory relief against government entities. This allows individuals and businesses to challenge government actions alleged to be outside lawful authority or in violation of the law or Constitution. However, the waiver has restrictions. Under Article I, Section II, Paragraph V(b)(4) of the Georgia Constitution, courts generally cannot award damages, attorney fees or litigation costs in such declaratory judgment actions unless specifically authorised by the legislature.The appeals court explained that the permitted relief under this constitutional provision is limited. A court may issue a declaration and subsequently grant an injunction to enforce that judgment, but the provision does not allow a plaintiff to use a declaratory judgment action to obtain monetary compensation. The judges found that Talon's request did not meet these requirements. Although the company sought a declaration that the tax deed was void, it also wanted Fulton County to reimburse the $220,000. The court further observed that Talon's request to invalidate the existing deed concerned rights that had already accrued. It did not involve uncertainty about future conduct that a declaratory judgment could resolve. Consequently, the company had failed to establish that the county's sovereign immunity had been waived.Appeals court sends case back for dismissal without prejudiceJudge Davis delivered the opinion, with Presiding Judge Doyle and Judge Whitaker concurring. The appeals court affirmed the trial court's decision to dismiss Talon's petition but disagreed with the dismissal being treated as one with prejudice. It explained that sovereign immunity is a question of subject-matter jurisdiction, meaning the court's legal authority to hear a case. A dismissal on those grounds does not decide the underlying merits of the dispute.The judges therefore remanded the case with instructions to enter an order dismissing the petition without prejudice. Importantly, the October 30 ruling did not determine whether the Atlanta parcel physically existed or whether the original tax sale was valid. It decided that Talon could not pursue the requested relief through this particular lawsuit because of sovereign immunity. The decision leaves the company's dispute over the $220,000 unresolved while reinforcing the limits on lawsuits seeking monetary relief from county governments in Georgia.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tennessee murderer captured over a week after escaping prison
articles.summary: Jacob Morley was serving a life sentence at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tennessee when he escaped by slipping through a fence on the property.
articles.body:
Authorities have captured a convicted murderer who evaded law enforcement for more than a week after escaping from a Tennessee prison. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation announced Tuesday that Jacob Morley was back in custody. He was arrested near Kansas City, Missouri, investigators said.

"Thank you to the public for your assistance, vigilance, and the tips provided during this investigation," the bureau said in a statement. "We also thank all of our law enforcement partners for their continued efforts to safely bring this search to a successful conclusion."

Missouri State Highway Patrol said it handled Morley's arrest alongside multiple partner agencies, after Tennessee authorities reported that Morley may be traveling through Missouri, based on footage obtained through Flock cameras. The arrest at around 11:30 a.m. local time near Norbone, a small city about an hour's drive from Kansas City, the state agency said.

Little information about the inmate's escape, and the multi-state search for him, have been made available since Morley broke out of prison. But investigators said more will be released as it becomes available.

Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence at the Northwest Correctional Complex in an isolated part of Tiptonville, a town roughly 90 miles from Memphis in northwestern Tennessee. He had been convicted of killing a coworker four years ago, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction.

Correctional officers discovered Morley was missing from the prison at around 11:30 p.m. local time on Oct. 25, the department said. While parsing security cameras later on, investigators said they saw footage of Morley escaping the complex, while wearing his prison uniform, by slipping through a fence on the property.

Authorities released additional security footage two days later that showed the inmate stealing a white 2008 Ford F-350, with Tennessee plates and a logo for Lindamood Planting Company on the side door, in the early hours of Oct. 27. It was stolen from Lake County, which includes Tiptonville, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said.

The truck was located later the same day in Marion, Illinois, which is about 150 miles north of Tiptonville, the investigative bureau said . Morley's whereabouts were unknown at the time.

The bureau had said earlier in the week that Morley was on its "most wanted" list, as various agencies, including the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, the governor's office and U.S. Marshals, offered combined rewards of up to $17,500 for information leading to his arrest.

Investigators haven't shared details about how exactly the inmate escaped, beyond the fact that he breached a fence at the prison.

Morley received a lifetime prison sentence for murdering Cody Birchfield, his former coworker, in 2022. Authorities said Birchfield's body was found in a box under Morley's home in Tennessee's Carter County after he had been missing for several weeks.

In addition to first-degree murder, Morley was convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest, as he fled when deputies arrived at his home in 2022. Authorities said the manhunt for him at the time ended in North Carolina.

Northwest Correctional Complex is a men's prison with the capacity to hold 1,776 inmates under varying degrees of security, from the lowest level up to maximum, according to the Tennessee Department of Correction. It also houses minors who have been convicted of crimes as adults.

Multiple violent incidents have taken place inside the prison in recent years, some of which involved attacks between inmates and prison staff. In July, a grand jury returned dozens of indictments over the murders of five inmates, assaults against staff and other acts of violence. At a recent meeting of the Tennessee Inmate Disciplinary Oversight Board, members discussed ongoing problems in the prison and suggested issues with leadership played a role.

articles.title: Scientist builds a mini universe of 24,000 atoms to show time can be measured without a clock
articles.summary: A scientist at the University of Birmingham has built a mini universe out of about 24,000 atoms to show that time can be measured without a clock.
articles.body: A scientist at the University of Birmingham has built a mini universe out of about 24,000 atoms to show that time can be measured without a clock. Giovanni Barontini's experiment tracks the order of events purely through changes in entropy, the measure of disorder in a system.The result matters because physics still has no settled answer on what time is. General relativity and quantum mechanics describe it differently, and this lab-made universe offers a controlled way to study that mismatch.The atoms are rubidium, chilled to almost absolute zero, which is around minus 273 degrees Celsius. At that temperature they stop behaving like separate particles and act more like a single cloud.The cloud sits in a trap it cannot escape. A specially configured laser splits the trap into two halves. One is the bright side, which was observed. The other is the dark side, which stays unobserved.Entropy, not a clock, keeps time in this mini universeOnly the bright side served as the timekeeper. Its entropy kept changing, and the internal timer moved forward only when atoms crossed the laser barrier between the two halves. By watching the cloud expand and contract, and by tracking the exchange of atoms, it became possible to work out the order in which events happened.There was a catch. When no atoms crossed over, the internal clock stopped. An external clock kept running anyway, so the two disagreed on when events took place. Inside this system, time did not match the time outside it.The experiment could help link relativity and quantum physicsBoth theories underpin modern physics, yet they do not always agree on how time works. In certain quantum systems, for instance, time can be reversed. Showing that time can be read from entropy changes in an atomic system is a step toward bringing the two together.Barontini's model is only a starting point. It leaves out factors such as black holes, and several settings can be changed, including the shape of the trap, the density of the atoms and the height of the laser barrier.The cloud's repeated swings between the dark and bright sides could also help scientists simulate conditions just after the Big Bang. It might even help model the lead-up to the Big Crunch, the theoretical point at which the universe collapses into itself.The full impact will take a while to show. For now, it answers a simple question: you do not need a clock to tell time, as long as something keeps changing.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'The Kite Runner' author Khaled Hosseini's foundation has educated 15,000 Afghan students and built 537 shelters for displaced families
articles.summary: Khaled Hosseini, the Afghan-born author of The Kite Runner, founded a non-profit organisation that supports vulnerable people in Afghanistan today.
articles.body: Khaled Hosseini, the Afghan-born author of The Kite Runner, founded a non-profit organisation that supports vulnerable people in Afghanistan today. The Khaled Hosseini Foundation says it has provided more than $2.2 million in grants, helping fund education, shelter, healthcare and economic opportunities for women. Its reported work includes building 537 shelters that house more than 3,200 men, women and children, as well as providing education for over 15,000 students.According to the Khaled Hosseini Foundation, it also helped fund an expansion of a maternity centre expected to assist in the delivery of 6,000 babies and care for roughly 33,000 women a year. Started in 2008, the organisation works through non-profit groups operating in Afghanistan.Khaled Hosseini Foundation focuses on humanitarian support in AfghanistanThe Khaled Hosseini Foundation was started by the award-winning author of The Kite Runner in 2008. It is registered as a 501(c)(3) non-profit organisation and says its work centres on humanitarian relief and shelter for families, economic opportunities for women, and healthcare and education for children in Afghanistan.Rather than describing itself as a direct service provider, the foundation says it funds grantees working on the ground. These organisations include established international aid groups with experience in conflict areas, some of which have worked in Afghanistan for decades. This approach helps ensure grants are used efficiently and reach vulnerable Afghans. Its mission statement places women and children at the centre of its work and overall grant-making priorities.Foundation reports 537 shelters and education for 15,000 studentsThe foundation reports that it has granted more than $2.2 million with support from donors. Its listed results include 537 shelters, which house over 3,200 men, women and children. Its work has provided education for more than 15,000 students. It also helped fund a maternity centre expansion. articles.title: FedEx was running out of money in 1973 when founder Fred Smith took its last $5,000 to a Las Vegas blackjack table and reportedly won $27,000 to help keep it afloat
articles.summary: Discover how Fred Smith transformed a $5,000 blackjack gamble into a $27,000 lifeline for FedEx, helping the company thrive in its early days against all odds.
articles.body: The stakes and competition in the business world have always been cutthroat, but rarely has a game of blackjack decided the survival of a company. For Fred Smith, however, a night in Las Vegas became an inseparable part of FedEx’s early history. With only $5,000 left and an urgent bill to meet, the founder gambled the money, per The Washington Post. The axiom of gambling has always been that the house always wins in the long run. The thumb rule is to cash out before that, but for Smith, the odds favoured his boldness. The return helped keep the company in operation; the real test, however, was turning an ambitious overnight delivery idea into a business that could pay its way.The gamble behind the success storyIn 1973, Federal Express was running out of financial runway to set off on its ambition. Its aircraft were flying, its delivery system functioned, and the company had started the onerous task of building an overnight parcel service. But the downside was that the company was burning through money faster than it had projected in return.According to The Washington Post, the company’s bank accounts were nearing zero, and Smith cashed in all the remaining $5,000 on a blackjack game at the time when the company needed $24,000 to keep its air fleet in operation. Smith ended up winning $27,000, which threw the company a lifebuoy that kept it afloat.The episode is a striking story of the quintessential American dream coming to fruition, retold from FedEx’s early years. But it can also distract from the harder problem that Smith had to navigate: making an overnight delivery system work as a commercial service.As the saying goes, it's easier said than done, because the reality was it would require substantial investment before it could yield dependable returns. FedEx began operations in April 1973, serving 25 American cities with a fleet of aircraft. The company had to establish routes, acquire customers and persuade businesses to depend on a service that was still unknown.A founder shaped by war and the company's highs and lowsSmith’s commitment to business had roots in his earlier life. He served in the US Marine Corps during the Vietnam War and completed two tours. After returning, he pursued the idea that had dawned on him at Yale. Unfettered by the financial and operational challenges that lay ahead, he started the company with some of his inherited family fortune. In a 1998 interview, reflecting on that experience, he said: “I was willing to take a chance, because losing wasn’t the worst thing in the world that could happen to you.”FedEx’s model depended on coordination. The idea he had while studying at Yale was rather simple in theory: create a central hub where parcels could be collected, sorted and dispatched to their destinations overnight. Rather than depend on a patchwork of existing transport routes, the company would oversee the process through its own established network of aircraft and ground operations.One complication for FedEx was that it could not upgrade its fleet to the larger Boeing 727 until 1978. The change came after years of sustained effort to persuade lawmakers to loosen their rules on air cargo. Access to the Boeing 727 gave FedEx the much-needed boost to expand its air cargo capacity. By 1983, the sky was the limit for the company; it had reported more than $1 billion in annual revenue and was set on expanding further.In 1984, the company decided to test Zapmail, an electronic document-transmission service. The company invested in the venture as businesses were looking for quicker ways to send documents. But the service failed to gain lasting traction and was discontinued. Its collapse proved to be a costly setback, as recorded in Harrison Smith’s Washington Post obituary. This experience served as a reminder that the company’s expertise in physical delivery didn’t automatically translate into success in a different market.The obituary also documents legal and corporate controversies from Smith’s career and details complications he faced during his time at the helm as chief executive.You use AI every day. articles.title: Raised in orphanages and foster homes, Tom Monaghan borrowed $900 with his brother to buy a Michigan pizzeria; he later traded a Volkswagen for full control of what became Domino’s
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable life of Tom Monaghan, who overcame a turbulent childhood in foster care to co-found Domino's Pizza. Learn how his entrepreneurial spirit and commitment to quality transformed a struggling pizzeria into a global fast-food empire.
articles.body: Kneading dough would later turn into an empire for Tom Monaghan, whose story started in the year 1960. Back then, he and his brother Jim borrowed $900 to buy a struggling pizzeria in Ypsilanti, Michigan. They took turns running the shop for eight months until Jim decided to call it quits. The payout for Jim’s share was the Volkswagen Beetle the brothers used for making their deliveries. Tom kept the pizzeria, then called DomiNick’s, as the sole controller of the business, which would come to be known as Domino’s Pizza.Monaghan’s childhood was a turbulent period of changing homes from one place to another. His father died on Christmas Eve 1941, when Tom was four. According to the Michigan profile, his mother was preparing to train as a nurse and, struggling to support two sons, placed Tom and his brother in foster care. At six, Tom went with Jim to St. Joseph’s Home for Boys in Jackson, run by the Felician Sisters. There he would grow under the care of Sister Berada, whom he described as a surrogate mother in his biography, Pizza Tiger.Building the pizza business Monaghan wanted to study architecture at the University of Michigan, but his grades and financial situation made that difficult. He served for three years in the Marine Corps until his brother Jim presented him with the idea of purchasing a pizzeria for sale in Ypsilanti. According toEntrepreneur, the brothers paid a $75 deposit and borrowed the remaining $900 from a post office union credit.After Jim left, Monaghan worked tirelessly in the shop, registering more than 100 hours a week. He reduced the menu, limited sizes and toppings, set ingredient standards and focused solely on delivery. The reasoning, recounted in Pizza Tiger, was that a carefully made Pizza would disappoint if it arrived cold. His operating instruction was simple and concise: “Always keep your eye on the operation”.In 1965, he changed the name of his pizzerias to Domino’s Pizza; the business would later grow into a global fast-food chain. But similar to any success story, his journey was mixed with hits and misses. He began franchising in 1967, and the chain found customers in college towns and military bases. The expansion continued, but the early push was poorly managed by Tom, who was still a rookie in this business. Per Entrepreneur, 32 new stores opened in the first 10 months of 1969, and almost all of them failed. Monaghan was left with a debt of $1.5 million in debt and relinquished control to a local businessperson to avoid bankruptcy.After the setback, he altered his expansion plans. He stopped opening stores for the sake of increasing the count, lowered his annual target and paid closer attention to site selection. As a result, the business then skyrocketed. The Michigan profile records an increase from 290 stores in 1980 to more than 5,000 by 1990.Selling the company and turning to education The success of Domino’s gave Monaghan the financial leeway to expand his portfolio outside the restaurant business. In 1983, he bought the Detroit Tigers baseball team for $53 million. This proved to be a sound decision; in the following year, the team won the World Series.Monaghan became deeply involved in public work; his charity work was guided by a staunch Catholic faith. Ave Marie University’s biography says he founded Legatus in 1987, an organisation dedicated to Catholic business leaders, and established the St. Thomas More Law Centre. He even gave up the Domino’s presidency in 1989 to invest more time in Catholic charities, while serving the company as Chairman and chief executive until 1998.The same year, he sold Domino’s to Bain Capital, keeping a minority stake, for an estimated $1 billion, according to Entrepreneur. Ave Maria University traces his educational project to Ave Maria Institute, which later became Ave Maria College and shifted its location to Florida, far from the original Ypsilanti pizzeria. Monaghan became the University’s founder and chancellor. He remained active there and went on to receive honorary degrees from 13 universities. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: After being rejected by employers and landlords because of their criminal records, 5 formerly incarcerated women built a $2.5 million food business and started buying properties together
articles.summary: Five formerly incarcerated women in Chicago who struggled to find jobs and secure housing because of their criminal records have built a successful food
articles.body: Five formerly incarcerated women in Chicago who struggled to find jobs and secure housing because of their criminal records have built a successful food business generating $2.5 million in annual revenue and begun acquiring properties together. Their journey, which started with a small commercial food venture, has grown into a network of worker-owned businesses and housing cooperatives offering opportunities to people excluded from traditional employment and housing markets. Through ChiFresh Kitchen and its expanding cooperative network, the founders are demonstrating how collective ownership can help people rebuild their lives while creating lasting economic opportunities.Five formerly incarcerated women built a $2.5 million food businessThe story began in 2018, when Chicago-based Upside Down Consulting and community organisers started developing a worker-owned food business involving formerly incarcerated women. According to VOLTS, the organisation's roots lie in this effort to create an enterprise that would give its workers ownership, control and economic security.By December 2019, 5 people had committed to becoming the founding worker-owners of ChiFresh Kitchen. Kimberly Britt, Edrinna Bryant and Renee Taylor were among the women who joined the founding group. They began meeting regularly to develop the business and establish how they would operate collectively.The University of Illinois explained that the business was led by five formerly incarcerated people and focused on providing freshly prepared meals to organisations including schools and nursing homes. Its workers were also its owners, giving them the ability to make decisions about the enterprise.ChiFresh Kitchen officially launched in May 2020, during the Covid-19 pandemic. As the crisis created an urgent need for emergency meals, the business secured contracts through community networks to supply food to pantries, churches, senior centres and transitional housing organisations, according to Next City.How cooperative ownership changed their working livesThe founders initially had little experience running a cooperative. They learnt how to establish policies, set wages, manage finances, recruit workers and make decisions collectively while developing the business.Next City reported that this arrangement also allowed responsibilities to be shared rather than placing the entire burden of managing a company on one individual. Workers could divide tasks such as hiring, finances, human resources and finding new business.For Kimberly Britt, cooperative ownership offered something particularly important after incarceration: a voice in the workplace. Rather than having to accept rules imposed by an employer, worker-owners could participate in deciding how their business operated.UIC's report highlighted how legal support helped ChiFresh establish a strong foundation. The university's Community Enterprise and Solidarity Economic Clinic assisted with registration, contracts, investment options and business certifications. This support helped the founders establish ChiFresh as a Limited Worker Cooperative Association under Illinois law.The business initially operated from rented commercial kitchen space but soon outgrew it.ChiFresh Kitchen expands from meals to property ownershipIn December 2020, ChiFresh acquired a vacant former grocery store on Chicago's South Side. The purchase was financed through a $350,000 loan from Shared Capital Cooperative, while renovations required additional funding from grants and loans.The renovation took nearly 2 years, and the company moved into its new headquarters in October 2022. According to Next City, its daily production capacity increased from 500 meals to 5,000 meals following the move.By 2025, ChiFresh Kitchen had reached $2.5 million in annual revenue. VOLTS also describes the business as generating approximately $2 million annually, providing freshly prepared, culturally relevant meals to institutions including the YMCA and Greater Chicago Food Depository.Why the founders started buying homes togetherBusiness success did not immediately solve another major difficulty faced by the founders which is finding somewhere to live.After leaving transitional housing, Britt repeatedly applied for rental accommodation but struggled to secure a home because of her criminal record. Next City reported that other ChiFresh worker-owners encountered similar difficulties, even after Cook County introduced legislation restricting landlords from automatically rejecting applicants with criminal backgrounds.The founders decided to address the problem themselves by establishing JumpStart Housing Cooperative.In 2023, JumpStart acquired its first property, a three-unit building in Bronzeville. Financial support included a $360,000 acquisition loan, a $200,000 zero-interest renovation loan and a $150,000 city grant, according to Next City.The cooperative subsequently expanded. It acquired a six-unit property in South Chicago in 2024 and an eight-unit building in Woodlawn in September 2026.VOLTS explains that residents collectively own their housing through the cooperative, sharing responsibility and decision-making. The model also helps members avoid the insecurity of relying entirely on traditional landlords.VOLTS creates more opportunities beyond ChiFresh KitchenAs demand for jobs and housing increased, the founders recognised that ChiFresh alone could not employ everyone seeking opportunities. They established VOLTS, short for Village of Leaders Thriving in Solidarity, to help create and support additional cooperatives.Registered as a nonprofit in November 2024, VOLTS provides business support, training, funding assistance and services that help cooperative members manage their enterprises. Its work also includes personal support, such as mental health and other services.The network has expanded to include CrossTreats, a healthy snack manufacturing cooperative, and The Handlers, a property management business. CrossTreats is developing a manufacturing facility, while The Handlers provides maintenance and management services for properties within the cooperative network.According to VOLTS, its worker cooperatives collectively employ more than 20 people, with more than 75% of workers also owning their businesses.A cooperative economy takes shape on Chicago's South SideThe network's growth has received substantial public and private backing. Next City reported that the cooperative ecosystem raised $3.8 million in grants and borrowed another $2.8 million for property acquisitions and renovations. Chicago has contributed significantly towards the grants.CrossTreats' manufacturing facility, whose groundbreaking took place in October 2026, represents another step towards expanding employment and local production. Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson attended the event, highlighting the city's support for community-owned businesses.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: British govt unveils new rules for obtaining permanent settlement
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from London: UK home secretary Shabana Mahmood unveiled new rules for getting permanent settlement in the UK on Monday following a
articles.body: TOI correspondent from London: UK home secretary Shabana Mahmood unveiled new rules for getting permanent settlement in the UK on Monday following a public consultation which elicited 200,000 responses.She announced that ILR (indefinite leave to remain) — which gives migrants unrestricted access to the labour market and access to public funds — would now have to be “earned” and “should not be automatic” simply because someone has lived in the UK for five years.The starting point for settlement will move to 10 years, with faster and slower paths available, she said.To “earn” settlement, a migrant must not have a criminal record; must speak English to a high standard; must not owe any debt to the UK govt; and must have a record of at least three years’ worth of National Insurance contributions.The five-year path will remain open to those earning above £50,000, as well as to doctors, nurses and teachers, and care workers who fulfil certain criteria.But those earning less than £50,000, who are not in these professions, will have to wait 10 years. This retrospective change has caused considerable anxiety to many Indian migrants who came to the UK presuming they would get ILR after five years. On top of that, student, graduate, and youth mobility routes will not count towards “earned settlement”.Pranav Brahmabatt, spokesperson for INSA UK said: “While we recognise govt’s right to manage immigration, these changes risk creating significant financial, emotional and professional uncertainty for thousands of international students, graduates and skilled workers. We believe it would be fundamentally unfair to disadvantage those already living and working here through changes to their settlement pathways.”Those earning over £125,000 will be able to apply for settlement after three years. Anyone who has breached immigration rules, eg overstayed their visa, or who has accessed public funds in the five years preceding their application, will only be able to settle after 20 years.Refugees who arrive on the new safe and legal routes will be able to get settlement after five years, but those who arrive illegally, such as on small boats, will have to wait 30 years.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1921, Wichita cook Walter Anderson and Billy Ingram launched White Castle with a $700 loan; their tiny burger stand helped shape fast food
articles.summary: Discover the origins of White Castle, the fast food pioneer founded by Walter Anderson and Billy Ingram in 1921, and how their innovative approach transformed the way Americans eat.
articles.body: Many Americans still associated ground beef with the unhygienic practices of the meatpacking industry in the early 1920s and not every principled consumer would touch a burger purchased from a street stand. It was a strange time to launch a restaurant based on little more than ground beef, onions and a hot griddle because of the reputation that hung over the entire enterprise. However, a little stand in Kansas accomplished just that and the way its founders overcame public scepticism became the blueprint for the later fast food sector.White Castle was started in 1921 by a Wichita fry cook called Walter Anderson and an insurance and real estate agent named E.W. Ingram (better known as Billy) with a $700 loan. The partnership turned a speedy cooking method into a standardised chain and the Kansas Historical Society cites Wichita as the birthplace of the fast-food business. Company lore has it that the debt was paid back in just three months.A cook with a new method Anderson was born in St. Marys, Kansas, in 1880 and began selling hamburgers from a streetcar body at a busy Wichita crossroads in 1916. The hamburger of the day was more like a big meatball and took forever to cook. Anderson spread the ground beef on a hot griddle and fried it with onions, cutting down on prep to a few minutes and giving the sandwich a taste that people remembered. His number of stands grew and by 1921 he was operating three and planning a fourth.Ingram, an insurance and real estate agent, was in business with Anderson over property and the two opened that fourth facility at 110 West First Street in March 1921. It was called White Castle number 4 because there were previously three older stands. What Ingram brought to the table was a way to win over clients who were hesitant about the product.Clean enough to trustIngram wanted the restaurant to be as clean as possible, according to the Ohio History Connection, which holds the White Castle corporate files. The building was white with gleaming stainless steel counters and staff had to meet stringent standards of dress and grooming. His pitch to Anderson was simple: call the place White Castle and run the cleanest restaurant in town. Hamburgers and coffee were 5 cents each.The standards didn’t stay local. Anderson introduced paper hats, paper-wrapped hamburgers, a food preparation handbook and requirements on employee cleanliness and appearance. The idea was consistency. A client should get the same product and service at every White Castle. A 1926 company newsletter reports that the company sold more than three million hamburgers and 48,000 gallons of coffee in 1925. Numbers like that made one stand in Wichita look like a lot more than one stand.From Wichita to a chainWhite Castle quickly opened a second location in Kansas City and, by the end of the 1920s, had spread to 12 major cities. Local newspaper coverage compiled by the Wichita State University Libraries gives a sense of the pace. By December 1925, there were 21 White Castles in all, five of them in Wichita and by April 1933 the company had 125 castles in sixteen towns.Anderson’s interest in the business faded as it grew, and Ingram bought him out in 1933. The following year, the headquarters moved to Columbus, Ohio, where it remains. The Ingram family still owns the company, now led by Billy Ingram’s great-granddaughter, Lisa Ingram and Nation’s Restaurant News reported in March 2026 that White Castle has about 340 restaurants in 14 states. In a twist, there are no White Castle restaurants in Kansas at all. That is how a cook with better burger-cooking skills and an insurance agent with great convincing skills helped define the overall American style of eating out.You use AI every day. articles.title: EC: Okay to use Form 6 for re-inclusion in rolls
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Election Commission Tuesday clarified that no action will be taken against a previous elector, whose name is deleted from draft rolls published
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Election Commission Tuesday clarified that no action will be taken against a previous elector, whose name is deleted from draft rolls published during Special Intensive Revision (SIR), who seeks re-inclusion by filling Form 6.The declaration that the voter's name is being included in the electoral roll for the first time will not be liable for prosecution under election laws for making a false statement, EC said in a communication to chief electoral officers (CEOs) of states and UTs.Recalling a Delhi HC order dated Oct 14 that held as "misplaced" the apprehension of an applicant, who argued that submitting Form 6 would amount to making a false declaration, EC directed that "no action shall be initiated under Section 31 of the R P Act by an ERO against an elector merely on the ground that the elector had been included in a previous electoral roll and has submitted Form 6 during the SIR process or afterwards, provided the elector is not already enrolled in any other parliamentary or assembly constituency and the declaration made is otherwise in accordance with law".Declaration prescribed under Form 6 has been in force since Aug 1, 2022: EC Stating that submission of Form 6 for inclusion afresh under SIR or afterwards is not, by itself, false merely because the elector was previously enrolled, EC on Tuesday instructed chief electoral officers of states and UTs that no action should be initiated by electoral registration officers (ERO) against such electors under Section 31 of the Representation of the People (RP) Act, 1950. Section 31 of the RP Act provides for imprisonment up to a year or fine or both, for anyone making a false declaration during preparation or updation of electoral roll.Certain previous electors, whose names did not figure in the draft electoral roll published during SIR, have been hesitant to submit Form 6 as they are also required to furnish a declaration prescribed in Form 6 that their name is being included for the first time in the electoral roll.They believe that this would amount to falsehood in view of their previous enrolment, attracting Section 31. Stressing that the declaration prescribed under Form 6 has been in force since Aug 1, 2022, the poll body clarified that an elector whose name does not appear in the draft electoral roll may submit Form 6 to seek inclusion in the final electoral roll, “in accordance with the prescribed procedure,” both under SIR and afterwards, irrespective of whether such elector was enrolled previously.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: An Arkansas couple divorced after 34 years of marriage, then fought four appeals over their business; a court upheld the wife's $183,000 half-share and interest from 2017, rejecting the husband's tax offset
articles.summary: A divorce can end a marriage, but disputes over a jointly owned business can keep former spouses in court for years.
articles.body: A divorce can end a marriage, but disputes over a jointly owned business can keep former spouses in court for years. In Arkansas, a couple who divorced after 34 years of marriage have been involved in four appeals over the division of their business, with disagreements involving its value, outstanding taxes and payments owed to the wife. Their latest legal battle has ended with an appeals court upholding the wife's $183,000 share of the business, along with interest dating back to the original divorce decree in 2017.In its October 28, 2026, decision in Craig Ballegeer v. Holly Ballegeer, available on Justia as 2026 Ark. App. 510, the Arkansas Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's order requiring Craig Ballegeer to purchase his former wife Holly's half-interest in their marital business, Groundskeeper. The court also rejected Craig's argument that he should receive credit for taxes he paid on behalf of both spouses. It upheld the award of 3.75% prejudgment interest from October 5, 2017, finding that Holly had been deprived of the use of her share while Craig retained and operated the business.How the business dispute continued after divorceCraig and Holly Ballegeer ended their 34-year marriage through divorce proceedings in Crawford County, Arkansas. Their original divorce decree, entered on October 5, 2017, valued Holly's one-half interest in Groundskeeper at $183,000. The decree also established a reverse-auction procedure to determine which former spouse would retain the business. However, disagreements over its division and the financial obligations associated with it led to repeated court proceedings.Craig challenged earlier decisions concerning the business, resulting in multiple appeals. In the third appeal, decided in 2024, the Arkansas Court of Appeals reversed an order requiring him to purchase Holly's interest. The court found that the lower court had incorrectly interpreted its earlier instructions and had failed to consider additional evidence about the business's value and debts paid by Craig during the intervening litigation.The case was sent back to the circuit court to reconsider how the business should be divided. The appeals court allowed several possibilities, including either spouse buying the other's share, dividing the asset equally, selling the business or making an unequal distribution supported by written findings.Court examines business value and unpaid taxesAfter the case returned to the circuit court, the parties presented additional evidence at an October 29, 2024, hearing. The proceedings examined Groundskeeper's value and profitability, Craig's payments towards Holly's share and the parties’ tax liabilities. Certified public accountant Cliff Hubbs testified that the parties’ actual tax liabilities, including penalties and interest, totalled $258,282. Craig had paid the entire amount. Hubbs calculated that Holly's half of those liabilities was $129,141.Holly acknowledged that Craig had paid the back taxes and that she had not contributed towards them. However, she maintained that Craig should retain Groundskeeper because he had already paid a substantial portion of its value. On December 10, 2024, the circuit court issued a letter ruling in Holly's favour. It found that Craig had controlled and profitably operated the business during the years of litigation and received most of its income.The court concluded that reducing Holly's property settlement to account for the taxes Craig had paid would effectively leave her with less than half of the marital property. It therefore required Craig to purchase her one-half interest for the original valuation of $183,000.Why the husband could not deduct the tax paymentsCraig challenged the decision, arguing that the circuit court had failed to follow the instructions given in the previous appeal. He also maintained that he should receive credit for the taxes he had paid on behalf of both former spouses. However, the appeals court found that the lower court had followed its earlier directions. It had considered the business's value, profitability, tax liabilities and Craig's payments before deciding how the asset should be divided.The previous ruling had allowed the circuit court to consider different methods of distributing the business. It had not required the judges to divide the tax liability equally or grant Craig the specific deduction he wanted. The appeals court also agreed that the lower court had considered the financial circumstances fairly. Since Craig had retained control of Groundskeeper and continued benefiting from its profits, reducing Holly's share by the tax payments would have given her less than her entitled portion of the marital assets.Court upholds interest dating back to 2017Craig separately challenged the decision to impose 3.75% interest on Holly's $183,000 share from October 5, 2017. He argued that no judgment requiring him to pay that amount existed when the original divorce decree was entered. The appeals court rejected this argument, explaining that prejudgment interest compensates a person for being deprived of money or property that should have been available to them.The judges found that Holly's half-interest had already been valued at $183,000 in the 2017 divorce decree. Although the reverse-auction procedure had left open which spouse would ultimately retain the business, Craig continued operating it and receiving its profits. The court also noted that Groundskeeper had remained profitable and that its earnings since the divorce exceeded the value of the entire business as determined in 2017. It therefore concluded that the value of Holly's loss and the date from which she was deprived of her share could be established. The circuit court was justified in awarding prejudgment interest from the original divorce date.Fourth appeal ends with ruling in wife's favourJudge Stephanie Potter Barrett delivered the opinion, with Judges Abramson and Murphy agreeing. The Arkansas Court of Appeals affirmed the January 20, 2025, order requiring Craig to purchase Holly's half-interest for $183,000. The lower court had credited him with 47 payments of $3,500, totalling $164,500, and calculated the remaining amount due, including interest, at $37,658.61 as of February 15, 2025.The decision brings another stage of the couple's prolonged business dispute to a close. It also clarifies that a spouse who retains and profits from a jointly owned business during lengthy divorce litigation may be required to compensate the other spouse for the loss of access to their share, including through prejudgment interest.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Mystery shrouds the status and whereabouts of Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) Commander-in-Chief Bashir Zeb Baloch, following an announcement by the rebel group on Tuesday that he was stepping down from his post. The announcement stood in contrast to claims circulating on pro-Pakistan military social media accounts that suggest an assassination attempt or his death.Rumours across pro-Pakistan Telegram channels, citing unnamed sources, speculated that Zeb was the target of a poisoning attempt by a close confidant in Kandahar and was subsequently rushed to a military hospital.Other accounts went further, claiming he was eliminated in a Pakistani military airstrike inside Afghanistan in September — a claim that remains independently unverified.Zeb had emerged as the primary face of the BLA's major offensive, Operation Herof. Visuals released during the operation depicting him riding a motorcycle without security cover had created significant ripples across security and intelligence circles.In an official statement issued by the BLA, the group clarified the context around Zeb's departure saying: "Following the decision of the Senior Command Council in accordance with the constitution of the organization, former Commander-in-Chief of the Baloch Liberation Army, Bashir Zeb Baloch, will no longer serve as the head of the organization.""Until the selection of a new Commander-in-Chief, all administrative, military, and policy-making powers have been officially entrusted to the Senior Command Council, the highest supreme body of the BLA, while military operations across all fronts will continue without interruption," the statement from BLA said.The rebel group saidnthat during the reorganization of the BLA in 2018, the ideological and structural founder of the BLA, Ustad Aslam Baloch, had brought an end to hereditary politics and lifelong leadership, establishing the organization on the foundations of merit, transparency, and institutional principles."He set the guiding principle that no matter how influential, prominent, or high-ranking a commander may be in this movement, no individual can remain Commander-in-Chief for life. To maintain this ideological and organizational continuity, a clear and consensus-based procedure was incorporated into the BLA constitution so that, if the need ever arose, an established and peaceful constitutional pathway for a smooth leadership transition would exist.""In accordance with this principle, a joint meeting of the highest bodies of the BLA was held on October 16, during which constitutional and organizational matters were thoroughly reviewed. During the meeting, all commanders unanimously decided in favor of leadership transition to impart fresh momentum to the organization's activities," the statement said."Our operational activities across all fronts continue without interruption. The name of the new Commander-in-Chief will be announced soon at the conclusion of the next phases," the BLA said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Largest monitoring effort in history’: Trump’s DOJ deploys 1,000 monitors; Democrats allege voter intimidation
articles.summary: The US Justice Department deployed around 1,000 election monitors and observers across the country on Tuesday, describing the move as the largest
articles.body: The US Justice Department deployed around 1,000 election monitors and observers across the country on Tuesday, describing the move as the largest monitoring effort in its history.The deployment covered jurisdictions in all 50 states, including several predominantly Democratic areas, and drew criticism from voting rights groups and Democratic officials who raised concerns about possible voter intimidation.According to Reuters, the monitors were sent to jurisdictions where Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris defeated President Donald Trump in about two-thirds of the areas in the 2024 election. Black and Latino voters make up a majority in many of these jurisdictions, which are concentrated in states that could determine control of the US Senate.Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K Dhillon defended the deployment, saying the department was pursuing election transparency in an “assertive and nondiscriminatory manner”.The Justice Department said its observers would monitor compliance with federal voting laws. However, they cannot conduct investigations at polling locations or prevent anyone from voting.The deployment came amid a legal dispute between the Trump administration and California over more than 20,000 mail-in ballots that federal officials alleged were likely issued to noncitizens. The Supreme Court rejected the administration's request to temporarily block California from counting the ballots on Monday night.In a series of subsequent rulings, the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals reversed its position and allowed federal officials to threaten election workers with prosecution over the handling of ballots suspected of involving noncitizens. The shifting decisions created uncertainty for local election administrators on polling day.California Attorney General Rob Bonta pushed back against the federal deployment, saying state observers would be present to monitor the federal monitors.Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass described the move as an attempt to intimidate voters and alleged that the administration was preparing to challenge election results if it did not get the outcome it wanted.Voting rights groups also questioned the department's approach. The NAACP Legal Defense Fund challenged the recruitment of sworn law enforcement officers as election monitors, arguing that their presence could intimidate voters. The department later removed several sworn officers from its pool of volunteer monitors.The expanded monitoring effort is part of a broader dispute over federal oversight of elections, with the administration arguing that stricter measures are needed to protect confidence in voting and critics warning that its actions could interfere with election administration and discourage eligible voters.You use AI every day.
